context.why: Everything built so far is invisible until somebody signs in as each role and sees what that person can do. Nothing in the framework creates a named account: there is one superuser from environment variables, a fake-data command for records, and nothing else. This story ships five accounts - one per role, one holding nothing - as part of the package, so that anyone building a portal on FairDM can load them into their own development environment and see the portal as a curator, as a community manager, as a developer, and as an ordinary contributor. They carry a password that is written down in the documentation, so the refusal to create them outside development is the whole of their safety, and a second check reports any that reached a production portal by some route the command never saw.
spec_sections: User Story 4 - Anyone building on the framework can sign in as each role
Key entities - the table of five accounts
plan_sections: Phases / Phase 4 - US-4, signing in as each role
prior_decisions: D7 - the accounts ship with the package, not with the demo. Their audience is wider than this repository: a research group building a portal on FairDM needs to sign in as a curator in THEIR portal, and the demo is not installed there.

D7 also settles the shape: a management command creating the accounts through the ORM, not a JSON fixture. Person subclasses a polymorphic Contributor, so a fixture row needs a content-type primary key that differs between databases; the password would ship as a pre-computed hash pinned to today's hasher parameters; and signing in without confirming an address needs an allauth EmailAddress row per account. A command hashes at run time, resolves content types by lookup, and can refuse outright - a loaddata of a shipped file cannot refuse anything.

D16 - the command's refusal guards the act of loading and not the resulting state, so a second check reports any of the five addresses found on a portal that is not in development. A database copied down from production, a dump restored the wrong way round, or an environment variable changed under a live database all produce the condition the command would have refused.

Check ids in fairdm/conf/checks.py are numbered by hundreds and E500 is now the portal-roles check. The development-accounts check takes fairdm.E501 - it is reserved and free. Read the file before you register anything.

The environment rule is the framework's own: fairdm.apps.NON_PRODUCTION_ENVIRONMENTS holds the environments FairDM ships a non-production override for, and everything else is a production deployment. Use that, do not invent a second rule, and do not key anything on DEBUG.

acceptance.given_when_then: Given a development environment with the roles installed, When the command runs, Then exactly five accounts exist - Portal Administrator, Data Curator, Community Manager, Portal Developer and Regular User, with the emails the specification's table gives, the first four in their matching role and the last in none. Each signs in through the portal with the password `password` and meets no confirmation step. Running it twice creates no duplicate. On the production baseline it fails, says why, and creates nothing. When one of the addresses already belongs to somebody, it fails rather than adopting that account.

Given fairdm/management/commands/create_dev_accounts.py, When it runs, Then it creates the accounts through the ORM, hashes the password at run time, marks each address confirmed so allauth lets them straight in, and refuses on any resolved environment outside NON_PRODUCTION_ENVIRONMENTS.

Given a production portal holding any of the five development addresses, When the check runs, Then it reports fairdm.E501 naming them; a development portal holding all five reports nothing; a database with no user table reports nothing, the same tolerance the portal-roles check carries.
Given fairdm/conf/checks.py, When check_dev_accounts_absent is registered, Then it carries id fairdm.E501 and the same tags as the portal-roles check, and no other check in the file shares that id.

Given a portal developer reading docs/portal-development/, When they look for how to sign in as each role, Then they find the command, the table of five accounts, the password, and a plain statement that these exist only outside production - and the demo's getting-started page points at it.
